fixes.explanation: Gibeah of Benjamin is the spot. Saul, Israel's king, has two thousand men at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and Jonathan, Saul's son, has a thousand with him in Gibeah (1 Samuel 13:2). I think a thousand men is plenty to keep a commander busy. Hold on to that name, because Jonathan's about to make some noise.
The Philistines did hear about the attack, friend, but they're not who Saul's horn is for. He says, “Let the Hebrews hear!” He's calling out to his own people.

False is right. The Philistines went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven (1 Samuel 13:5). Gilgal is where the people are summoned to join Saul (1 Samuel 13:4). So the Philistine camp is at Michmash, not at Gilgal.

Yes, the troops begin to desert Saul. He waited seven days for the time appointed by Samuel, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal (1 Samuel 13:8). I think a king watching his army walk off would feel that in his stomach.
No marching on Michmash here, friend. That's where the Philistines are camped. The text says the troops began to desert Saul (1 Samuel 13:8). They're leaving him, not charging anywhere.
That's the order. Saul says, “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings.” Remember he's been at Gilgal seven days, waiting. Keep an eye on what happens with the burnt offering.
That's the word. Samuel, the prophet, declares, “You have acted foolishly…” Samuel says it straight to Saul, with no wrapping on it. It's a heavy moment.

Wisely is the opposite of Samuel's word, friend. Saul gave his reasons about the deserting troops and the Philistines, but Samuel declares, “You have acted foolishly…” Then he points to the command the LORD gave Saul (1 Samuel 13:13).

Promise is close, friend, but Samuel's word is command. He says, “You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you…” A command is an instruction to follow, and a promise is a pledge someone makes. Samuel says Saul didn't keep the command.

Samuel is the prophet in this scene, but he never says the LORD picked a prophet. He says, “the LORD has sought a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people…” That's the description he gives.

False is right. Saul and Jonathan are in Geba of Benjamin, “…while the Philistines camped at Michmash.” The text has the Philistines camped there, not heading home. And the raiders are about to go out.

Three is right. Raiders went out of the Philistine camp in three divisions (1 Samuel 13:17). One headed toward Ophrah, another toward Beth-horon, and the third down the border road. That's three different directions.

That's the reason the text gives. The Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” So no blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel. That's a move aimed right at the forge.

Some Hebrews did cross the Jordan, but the text doesn't say blacksmiths did (1 Samuel 13:7). The reason it gives is that the Philistines had said, “The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears.” That's why there was no blacksmith to be found.
That's it. On the day of battle, not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. That's two people with weapons.

That would be a nice sight, but it isn't what the text says. Not a sword or spear could be found in the hands of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had weapons. The men with them had no sword or spear.
